basic.question: What is React Native, and how is it different from React for the web?
basic.answer: React Native is a framework for building mobile apps using React-style components and JavaScript or TypeScript. Instead of rendering to the DOM like React on the web, it renders to native UI components on iOS and Android. That means you use familiar React concepts like props, state, and hooks, but the target platform is a mobile app, not a browser.
basic.real_world: A team may choose React Native when they want one codebase for both iOS and Android but still need a real native mobile UI. It helps reduce duplicated work compared with building two separate native apps.
basic.follow_up: What kinds of things still need platform-specific code in React Native?

basic.question: What is the difference between a component and a view in React Native?
basic.answer: A component is a reusable unit of UI logic and rendering, while a View is the basic container component provided by React Native. Components can return Views, Text, images, or other components. In practice, you build your own components out of built-in primitives like View and Text.
basic.real_world: This matters when a junior developer tries to style everything with div-like assumptions from the web. In React Native, you usually compose screens from small reusable components instead of relying on HTML elements.
basic.follow_up: Why do Text elements behave differently from View elements in React Native?

basic.question: Why do you need to use the Text component for text in React Native?
basic.answer: Text must be rendered inside the Text component because React Native treats text as a special native element. Unlike the web, you cannot just place a string directly inside a View. If you try to render text the wrong way, you will get an error or unexpected layout behavior.
basic.real_world: A common beginner bug is putting labels directly inside a container and wondering why the app crashes. This shows up often when someone copies web JSX patterns into mobile code.
basic.follow_up: How does styling text differ from styling containers in React Native?

basic.question: What is the purpose of the StyleSheet API?
basic.answer: StyleSheet is a helper for creating style objects in React Native. It does not change what styles you can use, but it gives a cleaner structure and can improve consistency and maintainability. You pass the style object to the style prop, usually as an array if you need to combine styles.
basic.real_world: Teams use StyleSheet to keep screen styles organized and avoid large inline style objects scattered through the render method. It also makes it easier to reuse style values across components.
basic.follow_up: How would you combine multiple styles on one element?

basic.question: What is Flexbox used for in React Native?
basic.answer: Flexbox is the main layout system in React Native. You use it to control how components are arranged, aligned, spaced, and sized within a container. Most mobile layouts are built with flexbox instead of absolute positioning, because it adapts better to different screen sizes.
basic.real_world: This matters when building a screen that must look correct on small phones and large tablets. A flex-based layout is usually much easier to maintain than hard-coded pixel positions.
basic.follow_up: What is the difference between justifyContent and alignItems?

basic.question: How do props and state differ in React Native?
basic.answer: Props are inputs passed from a parent component, while state is data owned and changed by the component itself. Props should be treated as read-only in the child. Use props for configuration and state for values that change over time, like form input or toggles.
basic.real_world: This comes up when a screen needs to show a selected item or a text field value. If a junior puts everything in props, the UI becomes hard to update; if they put everything in state, components become harder to reuse.
basic.follow_up: When would you lift state up to a parent component?

basic.question: What is the difference between a ScrollView and a FlatList?
basic.answer: ScrollView renders all of its children at once, which is fine for small amounts of content. FlatList is designed for lists of many items and only renders what is needed on screen, which is much more memory efficient. For long lists, FlatList is usually the right choice.
basic.real_world: If a product list suddenly grows from 20 items to 2,000, using ScrollView can make the app slow or memory-heavy. FlatList helps prevent performance issues on lower-end devices.
basic.follow_up: What is a keyExtractor and why is it important?

basic.question: What does the key prop do in lists?
basic.answer: The key prop gives React a stable identity for each item in a list. It helps React update only the items that changed instead of re-rendering or confusing items when the list changes order. Keys should be unique and stable, not random values generated on every render.
basic.real_world: Bad keys can cause list rows to show the wrong data after insertions, deletions, or reordering. This is a common source of weird UI bugs in chat lists, todo apps, and feeds.
basic.follow_up: Why is using the array index as a key often a bad idea?

basic.question: How do you handle user input with a TextInput in React Native?
basic.answer: You usually make the TextInput controlled by storing its value in state and updating that state in onChangeText. That keeps the UI and your data in sync. Controlled inputs make validation, submission, and clearing fields much easier.
basic.real_world: This is used for login screens, search bars, and forms. If input is uncontrolled or handled inconsistently, the app can lose data or behave differently across platforms.
basic.follow_up: How would you clear the input after form submission?

basic.question: What is a common mistake when styling React Native components compared with web CSS?
basic.answer: A common mistake is using web-only CSS assumptions, like expecting every HTML tag or CSS property to work the same way. React Native uses a subset of CSS-like styling and its own components, so you need to check whether a style or layout approach is supported. Another common mistake is forgetting that layout units are handled differently and that text and containers are separate components.
basic.real_world: This often shows up when someone copies a web design into mobile code and the spacing or layout looks wrong. Debugging becomes easier once they understand the platform is similar to CSS, but not identical.
basic.follow_up: How would you debug a layout problem in React Native?

basic.question: What is the purpose of the SafeAreaView component, and when would you use it?
basic.answer: SafeAreaView adds padding so content is not covered by notches, status bars, or rounded screen edges on supported devices. You use it for top-level screens where important UI should stay within the visible safe area. It is mainly about layout protection, not general spacing. On some platforms and versions, behavior can differ, so it is not a substitute for careful screen design.
basic.real_world: Without it, a header or close button can end up under the iPhone notch or Android system bars. Teams often wrap whole screens in it to avoid device-specific layout bugs.
basic.follow_up: How is SafeAreaView different from just adding padding?

basic.question: Why do you need to use the source prop with Image, and what kinds of values can it take?
basic.answer: React Native does not render HTML image tags, so the Image component needs an explicit source. The source can be a local asset with require or a remote URI object. This matters because the shape of the value is not a plain string in the common case. A common beginner mistake is passing a URL string directly instead of an object with a uri field.
basic.real_world: Image bugs often show up as blank placeholders in production when remote avatars or product photos fail to load. Knowing the source shape helps avoid broken media across screens.
basic.follow_up: How would you handle an image loading error in React Native?

basic.question: What does TouchableOpacity do, and when would you choose it?
basic.answer: TouchableOpacity makes a view respond to presses by reducing its opacity while the user touches it. It is commonly used for buttons or tappable rows when you want simple visual feedback. It does not provide full button accessibility or complex gesture handling by itself, so it is a basic choice for simple interactions. For more advanced behavior, you would use a different touchable or gesture system.
basic.real_world: This is often used for list items, cards, and custom buttons. If you forget touch feedback, the UI can feel broken even though the tap works.
basic.code:
import { TouchableOpacity, Text } from 'react-native';

<TouchableOpacity onPress={() => console.log('tap')}>
  <Text>Save</Text>
</TouchableOpacity>
basic.follow_up: What is the difference between TouchableOpacity and Pressable?

basic.question: What is the purpose of the onPress prop in React Native?
basic.answer: onPress is the callback that runs when the user taps an interactive component. It is the standard way to handle button-like actions in React Native. You attach it to touchable components or buttons rather than to plain views. A common mistake is expecting any component to be pressable without adding an interactive wrapper.
basic.real_world: This matters for navigation, form submission, and list interactions. If onPress is wired incorrectly, the UI may look clickable but do nothing when tapped.
basic.follow_up: What happens if the handler is written as onPress={doThing()} instead of onPress={doThing}?

basic.question: How do you render a conditional UI element in React Native?
basic.answer: You usually use JavaScript conditions inside JSX, such as && or a ternary expression. This lets you show or hide parts of the UI based on state or props. It matters because React Native follows the same React rendering model, not a separate template language. A common mistake is trying to use statements like if directly inside JSX.
basic.real_world: Conditional rendering is used for loading states, empty states, and feature flags. If done poorly, the screen can flash the wrong content or crash on missing data.
basic.follow_up: When would you prefer returning early from a component instead of using a ternary?

basic.question: What is FlatList's renderItem function for?
basic.answer: renderItem tells FlatList how to display each item in the data array. It receives an object that includes the current item, and you return the UI for that row. This matters because FlatList is designed to render lists efficiently and needs a row renderer, not just raw data. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to pass a stable key extractor when item IDs are available.
basic.real_world: Teams use this for feeds, chat lists, and search results. If row rendering is not set up correctly, scrolling performance and item identity can suffer.
basic.follow_up: How would you add separators or headers to a FlatList?

basic.question: What is a StyleSheet in React Native, and why use it instead of inline styles everywhere?
basic.answer: StyleSheet lets you define reusable style objects in one place. It keeps component code cleaner and makes shared styles easier to maintain. Inline styles are fine for simple dynamic cases, but StyleSheet is better for repeated or larger sets of styles. The trade-off is a bit more indirection in exchange for readability and consistency.
basic.real_world: As screens grow, repeated inline styles become hard to scan and update. Teams often move common spacing, typography, and alignment rules into StyleSheet objects.
basic.follow_up: When would you still use an inline style in React Native?

basic.question: What does the placeholder prop do on a TextInput?
basic.answer: placeholder shows hint text inside the input before the user types anything. It helps explain what kind of value is expected, such as an email or password. It is only guidance and should not replace a label for important forms. A beginner mistake is using placeholder as the only instruction, which can hurt usability once the user starts typing.
basic.real_world: Forms often use placeholders for examples, but accessible apps still need visible labels. Otherwise users can forget what a field was for after entering text.
basic.follow_up: Why is placeholder text not enough as the only form label?

intermediate.question: How would you decide between using a controlled TextInput and keeping the value only in local state or a ref?
intermediate.answer: Use a controlled TextInput when the UI must always reflect app state, such as validation, formatting, or enabling and disabling actions. It is easier to reason about, but every keystroke updates React state and can add re-render cost if the screen is heavy. A ref or less controlled approach can reduce renders for very large forms, but you lose some immediate synchronization and validation simplicity. In most apps, controlled inputs are the default unless profiling shows a problem.
intermediate.real_world: This comes up in sign-up and checkout forms where you need to validate as the user types or auto-format phone numbers. Teams often switch a large form to a more optimized pattern only after seeing typing lag on older devices.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you debounce validation without making the input feel laggy?

intermediate.question: What happens if a FlatList item component changes identity on every render, and how do you fix it?
intermediate.answer: If item rows are recreated every render, FlatList can lose much of its performance benefit because memoization becomes less effective and more rows re-render than necessary. The fix is to keep row components stable with React.memo where appropriate, avoid creating new inline callbacks or objects unnecessarily, and pass only the props the row actually needs. If the row depends on changing outside state, make that dependency explicit rather than letting everything re-render by accident.
intermediate.real_world: This usually shows up in feeds or message lists where scrolling gets janky after a small state change elsewhere on the screen. A common cause is passing anonymous functions to each row from the parent.
intermediate.follow_up: When would React.memo not help much in a list?

intermediate.question: How do you choose between Pressable and TouchableOpacity for touch interactions?
intermediate.answer: Pressable is the more flexible modern choice because it exposes press states and lets you style based on pressed, hovered, or focused state. TouchableOpacity is simpler if you just want a basic opacity feedback effect. In new code, Pressable is usually preferred because it scales better to custom interaction patterns and accessibility needs, while TouchableOpacity can still be fine for straightforward buttons.
intermediate.real_world: Teams often migrate old screens from TouchableOpacity to Pressable when they need consistent feedback across tap, long press, and focus states. It also helps when building reusable button components with richer variants.
intermediate.follow_up: What accessibility behavior do you need to preserve when you build a custom pressable button?

intermediate.question: What is the role of a useEffect cleanup function in React Native, and what bug does it prevent?
intermediate.answer: Cleanup runs when a component unmounts or before the effect re-runs, and it is used to unsubscribe, remove listeners, or cancel async work. Without cleanup, you can leak event listeners or try to update state after the screen is gone. That causes duplicate events, warnings, and hard-to-track bugs when users navigate around the app. It is especially important for timers, subscriptions, and network requests tied to a screen lifecycle.
intermediate.real_world: This often breaks screens that listen to AppState, keyboard events, or device sensors. After navigating back and forth, the same listener fires multiple times because old subscriptions were never removed.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you handle cancelling a fetch request when the screen unmounts?

intermediate.question: How do you decide when to lift state up versus keep it inside a reusable component in React Native?
intermediate.answer: Keep state inside a component when only that component needs it and the behavior is self-contained, such as a dropdown being open or closed. Lift state up when multiple siblings need the same data, or when the parent needs to control it for validation, navigation, or persistence. Lifting too early makes components noisy and harder to reuse, but keeping shared state too low leads to prop drilling and inconsistent UI. The trade-off is local simplicity versus shared coordination.
intermediate.real_world: This comes up with forms, filters, and bottom sheets where several parts of the screen need to react to the same selection. If the state starts local and then spreads, teams often refactor it upward once the screen grows.
intermediate.follow_up: When would you introduce context instead of passing props through multiple levels?

intermediate.question: What is a realistic use case for React.memo in React Native, and when can it make things worse?
intermediate.answer: React.memo is useful for rows, cards, or controls that receive stable props but sit inside a parent that re-renders often. It can reduce unnecessary work and smooth scrolling or typing. It can make things worse if props change every render anyway, because you pay the comparison cost without getting a skip, or if you rely on memoization and accidentally hide stale data bugs. Use it where profiling shows repeated renders are expensive and props are mostly stable.
intermediate.real_world: A common example is a large product list where changing a search box should not re-render every visible row. On the other hand, memoizing every tiny component in a screen usually adds complexity without measurable gain.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you verify whether memoization actually improved performance?

intermediate.question: How do you handle navigation parameters safely when a screen depends on them?
intermediate.answer: Treat route params as input that may be missing or malformed, and validate or provide fallbacks before using them. If a screen cannot function without a param, fail early with a clear fallback UI rather than assuming it exists and crashing later. Keep navigation state and server data separate: the route can identify what to load, but the screen should still handle loading and error states. This makes deep links and app restores safer.
intermediate.real_world: This matters when users open a deep link directly into a detail screen. If the parameter is absent or stale, the screen should show an error or redirect instead of rendering broken content.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you model a screen that can be opened both from navigation and from a push notification?

intermediate.question: What is the difference between using useRef and useState for values that change over time in a React Native component?
intermediate.answer: useState triggers a re-render when the value changes, so it is for data that affects what the UI shows. useRef stores a mutable value across renders without re-rendering, which is useful for timers, previous values, imperative handles, or DOM-equivalent references. If you put UI data in a ref, the screen will not update when it changes, which is a common bug. If you put non-UI bookkeeping in state, you may cause unnecessary renders.
intermediate.real_world: This is common for tracking whether a user has already seen a modal, storing timeout IDs, or saving the latest callback for an event listener. Using the wrong hook often leads to stale behavior or extra renders.
intermediate.follow_up: When would you use useRef to avoid a stale closure?

intermediate.question: How do you debug a screen that is slow on older Android devices but seems fine in development?
intermediate.answer: First separate JS thread work from rendering and native performance by profiling where the time goes. Look for expensive re-renders, large lists without virtualization, heavy images, or synchronous work during mount, and test on a real low-end device because dev mode can hide problems. Remove console noise and debug tooling overhead before comparing. The main trade-off is that optimization only matters after you know whether the bottleneck is React rendering, JS logic, or native UI work.
intermediate.real_world: This is a frequent production issue because a screen feels fine on a flagship phone but drops frames on older Android hardware. Teams often discover the culprit is repeated rendering or parsing a large payload on the JS thread.
intermediate.follow_up: What metrics or tools would you use to tell whether the JS thread or the UI thread is the bottleneck?

intermediate.question: How would you test a component that conditionally renders different UI based on loading or error state?
intermediate.answer: Test the visible behavior, not the implementation details: render the component in each state and assert that the expected text, button, or fallback appears. If the component depends on async data, mock the data source and cover loading, success, and error cases separately. This catches regressions in state transitions, which is more valuable than only snapshot testing static output. Keep tests focused on what the user can see or do.
intermediate.real_world: This matters for screens that show spinners, empty states, retries, and error banners. A broken loading branch often goes unnoticed until a network issue happens in production.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you test that a retry button actually triggers a new request?

intermediate.question: How do you keep a FlatList fast when each row has its own local state or expensive rendering?
intermediate.answer: Keep row components small and stable, and avoid creating new inline functions or objects for every item if you can help it. If a row needs local state, make sure it is truly row-specific and not derived from parent state that causes the whole list to re-render. Use memoization for expensive rows, provide a good keyExtractor, and avoid nesting heavy views inside each cell. If the list still feels slow, windowing and simpler item layout usually matter more than micro-optimizing one component.
intermediate.real_world: This comes up in feeds, inboxes, or product lists where scrolling stutters on mid-range Android phones. Teams often discover the parent screen is re-rendering every row because one piece of state changes above the list.
intermediate.follow_up: What tells you that memoization is helping versus just hiding a larger performance problem?

intermediate.question: When would you use Pressable's pressed state instead of TouchableOpacity or custom animation code?
intermediate.answer: Use Pressable when the visual feedback can be expressed as a style change based on whether the element is pressed. It gives you a simple way to react to press, long press, hover, and other interaction states without wrapping content in extra components. TouchableOpacity is fine for a basic opacity fade, but Pressable is more flexible and usually the better default for new code. If you need richer motion, you may still add animation on top of Pressable.
intermediate.real_world: Teams often replace touchables in design refreshes because they need different feedback on iOS and Android. Pressable lets them keep one component while adjusting pressed styles per platform.
intermediate.follow_up: What accessibility concerns do you check for when building custom pressable controls?

intermediate.question: How do you handle asynchronous data fetching in a screen so you do not update state after unmount?
intermediate.answer: Start the request in an effect, track whether the component is still active, and clean up on unmount so late responses do not call setState. This prevents warnings and subtle bugs when users navigate away before a request finishes. If the API supports cancellation, use that rather than only ignoring the result, because it saves work and avoids wasted network activity. Also keep loading and error states explicit so the screen does not get stuck in an ambiguous state.
intermediate.real_world: This happens in detail screens where users tap between items quickly. Without cleanup, an older response can arrive late and overwrite the newer screen data.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you structure this if the same data is shared by several screens?

intermediate.question: What is the practical difference between using useEffect and useLayoutEffect in React Native?
intermediate.answer: useEffect runs after the render is committed, so it is the normal choice for data fetching, subscriptions, and non-visual side effects. useLayoutEffect runs earlier, after layout but before the screen is painted, so it is useful when you need to measure or synchronously adjust something before the user sees it. Overusing useLayoutEffect can hurt responsiveness because it blocks painting longer than necessary. In most app code, useEffect is the safer default.
intermediate.real_world: This matters when you measure a header, animate a shared element, or need to avoid visible flicker on first paint. Using the wrong hook can make a screen flash the wrong layout before correcting itself.
intermediate.follow_up: When would you avoid doing layout-related work in a hook altogether?

intermediate.question: How do you decide whether to store form state in React state, a form library, or refs in React Native?
intermediate.answer: Use React state when the UI needs to update on every change and the form is small enough to stay simple. Use a form library when you have many fields, validation rules, or repeated patterns that would otherwise become messy. Use refs only for values that should not trigger re-renders, such as the current text while typing in a debounced search field or imperative focus management. The trade-off is between simplicity, performance, and how much validation and submission logic you need.
intermediate.real_world: This comes up in sign-up flows, checkout screens, and support forms. A small screen can stay with local state, while a long form becomes easier to maintain with a dedicated form solution.
intermediate.follow_up: How do you handle validation feedback if the input value itself is stored in a ref?

intermediate.question: What causes unnecessary re-renders when you pass callbacks into many React Native child components, and how do you reduce them?
intermediate.answer: If a parent creates a new callback on every render, every child that receives it sees a new prop and may re-render even when its own data did not change. The usual fix is to memoize the callback with useCallback when the child depends on reference equality, and to keep the callback's dependencies as small as possible. But useCallback is not free, so only use it where render churn is actually a problem. The bigger win is often reducing how much state the parent owns.
intermediate.real_world: This shows up in long forms or item lists where typing into one field makes many unrelated children update. The UI feels laggy even though each child looks simple.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you tell whether a callback memoization is actually worth keeping?

intermediate.question: How do you debug a React Native screen that shows a blank area only on one platform?
intermediate.answer: First check for platform-specific layout assumptions, such as a component relying on web-like sizing or a parent not giving its children a height. Then compare props and styles on iOS and Android, because differences in text measurement, elevation, overflow, and safe area handling can change the result. I would also strip the screen down to the smallest failing layout and add temporary borders or background colors to see which container collapses. If the blank area is caused by a runtime error, inspect the device logs, not just the JavaScript console.
intermediate.real_world: Teams often see a screen render correctly in the simulator but blank out on one Android device family because a parent view has no height. Reducing the layout to a minimal repro is usually the fastest path to the bug.
intermediate.follow_up: What would you inspect first if the screen renders, but the content is clipped or hidden behind another view?

intermediate.question: How do you test navigation-dependent components without relying on the real device navigator?
intermediate.answer: Mock the navigation object or render the screen inside a test navigator so you can verify calls like navigate and setOptions. Keep the test focused on what the screen should do when a user presses something or when route params change, rather than trying to test the entire navigation library. For logic-heavy screens, separate the navigation-independent rendering from the part that reads params. That makes the tests more stable and easier to understand.
intermediate.real_world: This matters when a button should move the user to a detail screen or when a screen title depends on the current item. A small mock keeps unit tests fast and avoids brittle integration setup.
intermediate.follow_up: When would you choose an end-to-end test instead of a component test for navigation?

intermediate.question: What trade-offs do you consider when choosing between a single shared component and platform-specific components in React Native?
intermediate.answer: A shared component reduces duplication and keeps behavior consistent, but it can become cluttered with platform checks and edge cases. Separate platform-specific components can be cleaner when iOS and Android have genuinely different interaction patterns or layout rules. The key is to share the business logic and split only the presentation that truly differs. If the component is mostly the same, keep it shared and isolate the platform branches to the smallest possible surface.
intermediate.real_world: This comes up with headers, date pickers, and action sheets, which often behave differently across platforms. Teams that force one abstraction too early end up with a hard-to-maintain component full of conditionals.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you organize shared code so that platform differences do not spread through the whole codebase?

intermediate.question: How do you prevent a screen from becoming janky when keyboard input is involved, especially on Android?
intermediate.answer: Avoid doing heavy work on every keystroke, because keyboard events can trigger frequent renders and layout passes. Keep the input component controlled only as much as needed, debounce expensive filtering or validation, and make sure the screen can scroll or resize correctly when the keyboard appears. If touches stop working or elements shift unexpectedly, inspect parent containers, keyboard avoidance behavior, and whether the focused field is pushing the rest of the layout into reflow. The goal is smooth typing first, fancy behavior second.
intermediate.real_world: This appears in login screens, chat composers, and search bars. A screen that feels fine on iOS may jump or freeze on Android when the keyboard opens and closes repeatedly.
intermediate.follow_up: How would you measure whether the slowdown is from rendering, layout, or JavaScript work?

advanced.question: Can you explain how the old bridge differs from the new architecture in React Native, and why that changes performance characteristics?
advanced.answer: The old bridge batches JSON-serializable messages between JavaScript and native, which adds copy cost, scheduling delay, and makes high-frequency interactions like gestures or animations fragile under load. The new architecture uses JSI, TurboModules, and Fabric so JavaScript can call native code more directly and the renderer can coordinate updates with less serialization and fewer async hops. That usually lowers latency and startup overhead, but it also exposes thread-safety and lifetime bugs that the bridge used to hide. The trade-off is better throughput and responsiveness in exchange for stricter native module correctness and a harder migration.
advanced.real_world: Teams often feel this most in gesture-heavy screens: a feature is fine in development, then drops frames in production when JS is busy parsing data or logging. Migrating specific modules to TurboModules can remove bridge bottlenecks, but native crashes may appear if the module was relying on bridge-era assumptions.
advanced.follow_up: What kinds of native modules benefit most from moving to TurboModules first?

advanced.question: What actually happens when the JavaScript thread is blocked in a React Native app, and which parts of the UI can still keep working?
advanced.answer: If the JavaScript thread is blocked, React rendering, event handling implemented in JS, timers, and JS-driven animations stop progressing. Native-driven work can continue: the main UI thread can still draw existing views, some navigation transitions may keep running, and animations delegated to native or a worklet runtime can stay smooth. Whether the app feels frozen depends on which interactions require JS at that moment. This is why moving continuous gesture or animation logic off the JS thread matters on busy screens.
advanced.real_world: A common incident is a screen that parses a large payload or does expensive state normalization on focus; taps suddenly lag and spinners stop updating even though the app has not crashed. Teams often discover the UI thread is fine, but JS is monopolized for hundreds of milliseconds.
advanced.follow_up: How would you prove in profiling that the bottleneck is the JS thread and not layout or image decoding?

advanced.question: How would you reason about frame drops in React Native with the UI thread, JS thread, and render pipeline involved?
advanced.answer: I split it into where time is being spent: JavaScript work, layout and commit work, and main-thread rendering like image decode or view inflation. Missing 60 fps means you have roughly 16.7 ms per frame, so repeated work above that budget on either the JS or UI side will stutter; at 120 Hz the budget is even tighter. I look for whether updates are too frequent, too broad, or too expensive, then reduce the amount of work per frame or move it off the critical path. The key trade-off is feature richness versus predictable frame-time under worst-case devices, not just flagship phones.
advanced.real_world: In production, the same screen may be smooth on iPhones but janky on low-memory Android devices because decode, layout, and GC pauses stack together. Senior teams set performance budgets per interaction and test on slower hardware before shipping.
advanced.follow_up: What metrics or tools would you use to separate JS stalls from UI-thread stalls on a real device?

advanced.question: When would you choose Fabric-specific optimizations or architectural changes instead of just adding memoization to React Native components?
advanced.answer: Memoization helps only if re-rendering JS components is the dominant cost and props are stable enough for the comparison to win. If the expensive part is mounting lots of native views, deep layout trees, or frequent commits, Fabric-era improvements like reducing host component count, flattening view hierarchies, and avoiding unnecessary layout churn usually matter more. I treat memoization as a local optimization and architecture as the bigger lever. The trade-off is that architectural changes take more design effort but tend to scale better as screens become denser.
advanced.real_world: A feed item wrapped in multiple decorative Views may still jank even after aggressive React.memo usage because the native tree and layout work are the real bottleneck. Simplifying the host tree often gives a bigger win than chasing callback identity everywhere.
advanced.follow_up: How would you detect that host view count, not React render count, is the main problem?

advanced.question: What failure modes do you watch for when using Hermes in production, especially around memory and startup?
advanced.answer: Hermes usually improves startup and can reduce memory compared with shipping a larger JS engine, but it does not eliminate pressure from large heaps, retained closures, or oversized bundles. I watch for long GC pauses, memory growth from caches that never evict, and differences in error stacks or debugging workflows compared with other engines. I also validate bytecode generation and source maps in the release pipeline because engine-specific build issues can surface only in production builds. The trade-off is better mobile-oriented runtime behavior, with some ecosystem and tooling differences to account for.
advanced.real_world: Teams sometimes fix startup time with Hermes and then still get OOMs on image-heavy flows because decoded bitmaps and retained JS references dominate memory, not the engine choice alone. Release-only crashes can also show up if source maps or bytecode artifacts are mismatched.
advanced.follow_up: How would you investigate a memory leak that appears only after navigating through several screens on Hermes release builds?

advanced.question: How do you design a native module boundary so it scales under high call volume instead of becoming a bridge or JSI bottleneck?
advanced.answer: I try to minimize chatty APIs and cross-runtime object churn by batching operations, using coarse-grained methods, and pushing repeated work to the native side when it does not need React state every step. For data streams, I prefer pull or chunked delivery over emitting thousands of tiny events, and I make lifecycle ownership explicit so listeners and native resources are cleaned up deterministically. With JSI, direct access is powerful but easy to misuse if object lifetime or thread affinity is vague. A fast boundary is usually one with fewer crossings and clearer ownership, not just lower per-call overhead.
advanced.real_world: This matters in modules like sensors, media, and local databases, where naive per-record callbacks can flood the app and create backlog or battery drain. Teams often redesign APIs after seeing that the module works functionally but collapses under sustained throughput.
advanced.follow_up: What would a better API look like for streaming thousands of database rows to JavaScript?

advanced.question: What are the real trade-offs between JS-driven animations, native-driven animations, and worklet-based approaches in React Native?
advanced.answer: JS-driven animations are simplest when they depend on app state already in JS, but they hitch whenever the JS thread is busy. Native-driven or worklet-based approaches keep per-frame work off the JS thread, which is much better for gestures and continuous motion, but they introduce constraints on what code can run and how state is shared back to React. The choice is mostly about determinism under load versus flexibility and debuggability. For touch-coupled interactions, I default to keeping the hot path off JS and syncing only meaningful state changes back.
advanced.real_world: A drag interaction that feels perfect in a simulator can become unusable on mid-range Android once network parsing and analytics are active on the JS thread. Moving the gesture and interpolation off JS usually fixes the visible stutter without changing the business logic.
advanced.follow_up: What bugs appear when animation state and React state drift apart, and how do you prevent that?

advanced.question: How would you handle a production incident where a React Native app sometimes shows stale data after backgrounding and resuming, even though requests are successful?
advanced.answer: I would suspect a race between screen lifecycle, cache invalidation, and out-of-order async completions rather than the network itself. The fix is usually to define freshness rules explicitly, tie requests to a request id or abort signal, ignore late results from older fetches, and revalidate on foreground or focus with deduplication. I also check whether state is restored from persistence before fresh data arrives and whether optimistic updates are overwriting newer server state. The important trade-off is freshness versus battery and bandwidth, but correctness comes first when resume paths are involved.
advanced.real_world: This happens in apps with persisted query caches or tabs left open for hours: users resume and briefly see yesterday's content, or an older response wins after a newer refresh. Without request versioning, the bug is intermittent and hard to reproduce.
advanced.follow_up: How would you extend that pattern if multiple independent resources on the screen can refresh concurrently?

advanced.question: What are the hard parts of using React 18-style concurrent rendering concepts in React Native, and what should engineers not assume?
advanced.answer: The main thing not to assume is that rendering work in React being interruptible means your side effects, native module calls, or UI updates are automatically safe to run multiple times or out of order. Concurrent rendering changes when and how renders are prepared, but commits still need to interact correctly with native state, and code that leaks effects or depends on render timing becomes more fragile. I keep render pure, make effects idempotent, and avoid coupling native operations directly to speculative renders. The trade-off is smoother scheduling for urgent versus non-urgent updates, but only if the app already follows React's correctness rules tightly.
advanced.real_world: A team may adopt transitions and then hit bugs where analytics, focus calls, or imperatively opened native views happen twice because the code assumed a one-render-one-side-effect model. These bugs are subtle because they often appear only under load or in development strictness modes.
advanced.follow_up: Which kinds of side effects in React Native are most dangerous if a render is restarted or delayed?

advanced.question: Suppose you have a very large feed with images, ads, and live-updating badges; how would you tune virtualization beyond the basic FlatList props?
advanced.answer: I start by reducing variability: stable item heights where possible, predictable image dimensions, and isolating live-updating subtrees so a badge update does not invalidate the whole row. Then I tune batching and windowing based on measured blanking versus memory, and I check whether ad SDK views or autoplay media are forcing expensive mounts on the main thread. For extreme cases, I consider alternative list implementations optimized for recycling and layout prediction, but only after proving FlatList is the bottleneck. The trade-off is memory versus scroll smoothness, and the right balance differs a lot between high-end and low-end devices.
advanced.real_world: On content-heavy feeds, teams often fix re-renders and still see blank cells because image decode, unpredictable row measurement, or heavyweight embedded native views dominate. Ads and live counters are common offenders because they update frequently and break assumptions about row stability.
advanced.follow_up: What signals tell you the problem is poor virtualization settings versus expensive row content?

advanced.question: How does React Native batch layout and mounting work under Fabric, and what kinds of bugs appear when code assumes mount is synchronous?
advanced.answer: Under Fabric, React computes a tree, Yoga calculates layout, and native mounting is committed in batches rather than each prop change immediately mutating native views. That means code that reads layout or calls imperative native APIs right after setState can observe stale or not-yet-mounted views. The fix is to rely on layout callbacks, refs after commit, or explicit synchronization points instead of assuming render equals mounted. This matters more with concurrent rendering because work can be interrupted and committed later.
advanced.real_world: A common production bug is measuring a just-opened bottom sheet immediately after toggling state, getting zero height on some devices and only intermittently under load.
advanced.follow_up: If you need to measure a view for an animation, what sequencing would you use so it works reliably across devices?

advanced.question: When would you use FlashList, RecyclerListView, or a custom native-backed list instead of FlatList, and what are the trade-offs?
advanced.answer: I’d start with FlatList, but switch when item count, heterogeneity, or update frequency makes JS-side cell management too expensive. FlashList improves estimation and recycling with a familiar API, while RecyclerListView gives more explicit control over layouts and recycling at the cost of complexity. A custom native-backed list can win for extreme feeds, but you pay in duplicated logic, harder debugging, and feature parity work across platforms. The decision is usually driven by frame stability, memory use, and how predictable row heights are.
advanced.real_world: Teams hit this with marketplace or social feeds where hundreds of rich rows, autoplay media, and ad insertions make simple FlatList tuning stop helping.
advanced.follow_up: What measurements would convince you that FlatList is no longer the right choice?

advanced.question: How do you prevent memory blowups in a React Native app that displays lots of remote images over a long session?
advanced.answer: The main levers are reducing decode size, limiting how many images stay mounted, and making cache policy explicit. Large source images can decode to far more memory than their on-screen size, so resizing on the server or requesting size-appropriate variants usually matters more than JS tweaks. You also want aggressive recycling in lists, placeholder strategies that do not keep multiple full bitmaps around, and to watch for leaks from retained screen trees or image references. Memory issues often show up after 10 to 20 minutes of scrolling, not in short local tests.
advanced.real_world: In production, apps often look fine on flagship phones but get killed on mid-range Android devices after a user scrolls a feed, opens detail screens, then returns several times.
advanced.follow_up: What would you inspect first if Android users report out-of-memory crashes after image-heavy browsing?

advanced.question: What happens when a React Native app receives a burst of native events faster than JavaScript can process them, and how do you design around that?
advanced.answer: If native emits events faster than the JS side can consume, queues grow, latency rises, and you start processing stale information. For high-frequency sources like scroll, sensors, or streaming updates, you usually need coalescing, throttling, sampling, or moving the hot path off the JS thread. The boundary should carry the minimum data needed, and expensive per-event object creation should be avoided. Otherwise you get jank, battery drain, and sometimes memory pressure from queued events.
advanced.real_world: This shows up with live maps, telemetry dashboards, or custom gestures where every native update is forwarded to JS and the app falls behind during interaction.
advanced.follow_up: How would your strategy differ for a gesture stream versus business events like order status updates?

advanced.question: How do you reason about startup time in React Native, and what changes actually move the needle versus just shifting work around?
advanced.answer: Startup is a pipeline: process launch, native initialization, JS engine startup, bundle load, module evaluation, first render, and first meaningful content. The biggest wins usually come from deferring non-critical module work, trimming eager imports, reducing synchronous initialization, and making the first screen cheap. Preloading can help, but only if it does not compete with first render or inflate memory. I separate cold start, warm start, and resume because fixes for one can hurt another.
advanced.real_world: A common mistake is moving expensive work from a splash screen into top-level module imports, which keeps the app looking busy but does not improve time to interactive.
advanced.follow_up: How would you detect whether startup cost is coming from bundle evaluation versus native initialization?

advanced.question: What are the trade-offs of using multiple JavaScript runtimes or surfaces in a large React Native app?
advanced.answer: Multiple surfaces can isolate features and improve ownership boundaries, but each runtime or independently initialized surface can increase memory, startup cost, and cross-surface coordination complexity. Shared caches, navigation state, auth state, and event delivery become harder when you no longer have one obvious in-memory world. The benefit is that teams can load code on demand and sometimes avoid one giant monolith, but you need strong contracts at the boundaries. I only do it when organizational or performance data justifies the complexity.
advanced.real_world: This comes up in super-apps or apps embedding React Native incrementally into many native screens, where every surface booting its own world can quietly consume a lot of RAM.
advanced.follow_up: If you had to share auth and feature flags across multiple surfaces, how would you avoid race conditions at startup?

advanced.question: Can you explain a case where React Native rendering looks correct in development but breaks in release builds, and how you would investigate it?
advanced.answer: Release builds change timing, optimization, logging, and sometimes engine behavior, so races and thread-sensitive bugs often appear only there. I look for code relying on dev-only slowdowns, unhandled promise timing, missing ProGuard or linker configuration for native modules, and assumptions hidden by development warnings or remote debugging. The investigation starts with a reproducible release build, symbolicated native crashes if any, and lightweight telemetry around app state transitions. You need to prove whether it is a JS logic bug, a native integration issue, or a build configuration problem.
advanced.real_world: Teams frequently see startup crashes or blank screens only in release because a native dependency was stripped or because dev mode masked an initialization race.
advanced.follow_up: What telemetry would you add first if users report an occasional blank screen only in production?

advanced.question: How would you make offline writes robust in a React Native app when the app can be backgrounded or killed at any point?
advanced.answer: I’d model writes as durable operations with ids, persisted intent, and explicit retry state rather than as in-memory promises tied to one screen. The client should optimistically update only when it can reconcile later, persist the mutation queue, and make operations idempotent so retries do not duplicate side effects. Backgrounding and termination mean you cannot assume completion callbacks will run, so recovery on next launch is part of the design. Conflict handling matters as much as transport reliability.
advanced.real_world: This matters in field apps where users create records with poor connectivity; without durable mutation logs, data appears saved locally but is silently lost after the OS kills the app.
advanced.follow_up: How would you handle a server response that rejects a queued offline mutation because the base record has changed?

advanced.question: What is your strategy for avoiding expensive unnecessary work when app state, feature flags, or global stores update frequently in React Native?
advanced.answer: The core idea is to reduce fan-out: subscribe as narrowly as possible, derive stable slices, and avoid rerendering large trees for state that only a few leaves need. Contexts that carry rapidly changing values can become a broadcast mechanism, so selectors or store subscriptions are often better than one giant provider. I also watch for expensive recomputation during render and for navigation stacks keeping inactive screens subscribed. The right architecture is usually more important than micro-optimizing individual components.
advanced.real_world: A production symptom is typing lag or dropped frames because a global store update causes hidden tabs, headers, and long lists to all rerender on every keystroke.
advanced.follow_up: What would make you choose context with selectors, Redux-style subscriptions, or a lighter external store?

advanced.question: How do you approach crash and ANR debugging in React Native when the issue crosses JavaScript and native boundaries?
advanced.answer: I treat it as a distributed failure across runtimes: correlate JS errors, native crashes, ANRs, device state, and what screen or action was active. Symbolication and native stack traces tell you where the process died or hung, while JS breadcrumbs and performance markers tell you what the app was trying to do. ANRs are often about main-thread blocking from native work, synchronous I/O, or pathological view inflation rather than a simple JS exception. The goal is to reconstruct the timeline, not to assume the top stack frame is the root cause.
advanced.real_world: In real incidents, a harmless-looking JS action like opening a modal can trigger native image decoding or database work on the wrong thread and cause Android ANRs on lower-end devices.
advanced.follow_up: What breadcrumbs or markers would you add so a future cross-boundary crash is diagnosable within one release cycle?
